questions.q: When the principal said, "We cannot turn a blind eye to lateness any longer," he meant that the school would now —
options: allow students to come late occasionally
deal firmly with students who arrive late
install lights to help late students find their way
questions.explanation: "Turn a blind eye" means to ignore. Saying they cannot do that means they will stop ignoring the problem and take action. The other options misread the idiom (ignore or allow) or take it literally (install lights).

questions.q: If someone advises you to "bite the bullet" before speaking to a difficult boss, they are telling you to —
options: face the unpleasant task bravely and get it over with
prepare extensively and delay the meeting
avoid the boss until the problem disappears
use flattery to soften the boss first
questions.explanation: "Bite the bullet" means to accept and face a painful or difficult action without delay. The wrong answers suggest avoidance, delay, or manipulation, which are contrary to the idiom's meaning.

questions.q: When a friend says, "After the exam I was on cloud nine," they are expressing that they felt —
questions.explanation: "On cloud nine" is an idiom meaning extremely happy or elated. The other options give unrelated emotional or physical states, so they are incorrect.

questions.q: In the sentence, "The new policy will iron out the problems," the verb 'iron out' means to —
options: smooth away difficulties or resolve them
questions.explanation: 'Iron out' figuratively means to eliminate obstacles or settle difficulties. The wrong options confuse it with worsening, concealing, or creating problems, which do not match the idiom.

questions.q: Choose the best word to complete the sentence: "The governor's speech was long, but it lacked any real __________ to convince voters that change was coming."
questions.explanation: "Substance" is the natural collocation here meaning real content or weight. "Substantiality" is uncommon and awkward; "substantiation" implies providing proof rather than general content; "subjugation" is irrelevant (means domination).

questions.q: Select the correct option to complete this sentence: "If he ______ earlier, he would not have missed the 8:00am meeting."
questions.explanation: This is a third conditional structure referring to a past unreal condition: "If he had left earlier, he would not have missed..." Simple past (left) or present perfect (has left) are incorrect here, and "would leave" misforms the condition.

questions.passage: Every market day in Onitsha, Mrs. Okoro arrived at sunrise with a lorry full of yams. She had inherited the trade from her father and knew the customers by name. Last week a heavy rain ruined part of her stock and the generator failed, causing a long blackout. Despite the losses, she refused to blame fate. Instead, she borrowed N20,000 from a cooperative and repaired the generator. By the next market day she was back, smiling and selling once more. Her regulars praised her determination; some even insisted on buying a little extra to help her recover.
questions.q: What does the passage suggest was Mrs. Okoro's immediate response to the losses she suffered?
options: She sold all her remaining yams at a huge discount
She gave up and closed her stall permanently
She blamed fate and waited for help
She borrowed money and repaired the generator
questions.explanation: The passage states she borrowed N20,000 and repaired the generator, which shows action rather than giving up or blaming fate. There is no mention of closing permanently or selling everything at a huge discount.

questions.passage: Every market day in Onitsha, Mrs. Okoro arrived at sunrise with a lorry full of yams. She had inherited the trade from her father and knew the customers by name. Last week a heavy rain ruined part of her stock and the generator failed, causing a long blackout. Despite the losses, she refused to blame fate. Instead, she borrowed N20,000 from a cooperative and repaired the generator. By the next market day she was back, smiling and selling once more. Her regulars praised her determination; some even insisted on buying a little extra to help her recover.
questions.q: Which phrase from the passage shows that Mrs. Okoro had good relationships with her customers?
questions.explanation: "Knew the customers by name" directly indicates a close relationship. The other phrases refer to when she arrived, how she obtained funds, and an effect of the generator failure; none indicate relationships.

questions.passage: Every market day in Onitsha, Mrs. Okoro arrived at sunrise with a lorry full of yams. She had inherited the trade from her father and knew the customers by name. Instead, she borrowed N20,000 from a cooperative and repaired the generator. By the next market day she was back, smiling and selling once more. Her regulars praised her determination; some even insisted on buying a little extra to help her recover.
questions.q: What is the tone of the passage toward Mrs. Okoro?
questions.explanation: The passage highlights her determination and how customers supported her, which creates an admiring and sympathetic tone. It does not criticize, envy, or show indifference toward her.

questions.passage: Every market day in Onitsha, Mrs. Okoro arrived at sunrise with a lorry full of yams. She had inherited the trade from her father and knew the customers by name. Last week a heavy rain ruined part of her stock and the generator failed, causing a long blackout. Despite the losses, she refused to blame fate. Instead, she borrowed N20,000 from a cooperative and repaired the generator. By the next market day she was back, smiling and selling once more. Her regulars praised her determination; some even insisted on buying a little extra to help her recover.
questions.q: Why did some of Mrs. Okoro's regulars buy extra yams?
options: To help her recover after her losses
Because the blackouts made the yams taste better
Because the extra yams were cheaper
To sell them in another market the same day
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says customers insisted on buying a little extra to help her recover. There is no mention of lower price, reselling elsewhere, or any effect of blackout on taste.

questions.q: Which word is stressed on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: 'Become' is stressed on the second syllable: be-COME. 'Danger' is stressed on the first syllable (DAN-ger), 'market' on the first (MAR-ket), and 'camera' on the first (CAM-er-a).

questions.q: Choose the best antonym of 'sparse' as used to describe a village population.
questions.explanation: 'Sparse' means thinly spread or few in number; its antonym is 'dense', meaning closely packed or many. 'Scattered', 'meagre', and 'thin' are synonyms or near-synonyms of 'sparse', not opposites.

questions.q: Which of the following contains the same vowel sound as the underlined 'o' in 'come' ("come")?
questions.explanation: In 'come' the vowel is the short /ʌ/ (as in 'some'). 'Some' matches that sound. 'Cone' and 'cove' have the long /oʊ/ sound, and 'calm' has /ɑː/ (in many Nigerian accents) or /ɑ/ which is different.

questions.passage: Mr. Musa opened a small bookshop in Zaria ten years ago. He kept regular hours and sold both school textbooks and storybooks. During the pandemic the shop closed for three months, but when it reopened he noticed customers coming earlier and buying in larger quantities. He had expected a drop in sales, yet revenue increased. Last month he decided to hire an extra assistant to help with restocking. His neighbours praise him for always giving a discount to students.
questions.q: Which sentence from the passage shows that the increase in sales was unexpected?
options: Mr. Musa opened a small bookshop in Zaria ten years ago.
He had expected a drop in sales, yet revenue increased.
During the pandemic the shop closed for three months, but when it reopened he noticed customers coming earlier and buying in larger quantities.
Last month he decided to hire an extra assistant to help with restocking.
questions.explanation: The sentence 'He had expected a drop in sales, yet revenue increased.' explicitly states his expectation (a drop) and contrasts it with the actual outcome (increase), showing surprise. The other sentences state facts without indicating expectation versus outcome.

questions.passage: Mr. Musa opened a small bookshop in Zaria ten years ago. He kept regular hours and sold both school textbooks and storybooks. During the pandemic the shop closed for three months, but when it reopened he noticed customers coming earlier and buying in larger quantities. He had expected a drop in sales, yet revenue increased. Last month he decided to hire an extra assistant to help with restocking. His neighbours praise him for always giving a discount to students.
questions.q: Which verb tense is used in 'he had expected a drop in sales'?
questions.explanation: 'He had expected' is past perfect, used to show an action completed before another past action or time. Simple past would be 'he expected', past continuous would be 'he was expecting', and present perfect would be 'he has expected'.

questions.passage: Mr. Musa opened a small bookshop in Zaria ten years ago. He kept regular hours and sold both school textbooks and storybooks. During the pandemic the shop closed for three months, but when it reopened he noticed customers coming earlier and buying in larger quantities. He had expected a drop in sales, yet revenue increased. Last month he decided to hire an extra assistant to help with restocking. His neighbours praise him for always giving a discount to students.
questions.q: In the passage, which word is closest in meaning to 'revenue'?
questions.explanation: 'Revenue' refers to the income from business activities; here 'sales' is the closest match. 'Discount' is a price reduction, 'stocking' refers to filling shelves, and 'neighbours' are nearby people—none mean income.

questions.q: Which sentence uses emphatic stress to contradict a suggestion that Mr. Ahmed was absent?
options: He would be absent if sick.
questions.explanation: Emphatic stress is used to contradict or emphasise; 'He was there, not absent.' directly emphasises presence and contradicts the suggestion of absence. The other options either ask a question or speculate and do not provide emphatic contradiction.

questions.q: Choose the correct form to complete the sentence: "If Aisha _______ earlier, she would have caught the 6:00 Lagos bus."
questions.explanation: This is a third conditional referring to a past unreal situation; the correct structure is 'If' + past perfect (had left) + would have + past participle. 'Left' (simple past) or 'was leaving' (past continuous) are incorrect for this conditional, and 'has left' is present perfect.

questions.q: Which word rhymes with the vowel sound in the underlined 'o' of 'go' ("go")?
questions.explanation: 'Go' contains the diphthong /oʊ/ (as in 'show'), so 'show' rhymes. 'Got' has /ɒ/ or /ɑ/ depending on accent and does not rhyme, 'soak' has /oʊk/ but with a following consonant cluster causing different vowel length; 'sow' can be pronounced the same in some accents but is often /saʊ/ (rhyming with 'cow'), making 'show' the best choice.

questions.q: Choose the correct form of the word to complete the sentence: "The committee praised Amina for her __________ in resolving the dispute quickly."
questions.explanation: The noun that fits the sentence is 'diplomacy' (skill in dealing with people). 'Diplomatically' is an adverb, which doesn't fit the noun slot; 'diplomacity' and 'diplomaticness' are nonstandard or incorrect formations.

questions.q: Select the correct word to complete the sentence: "After the flood the villagers faced a shortage of ________ facilities, so the council sent portable toilets."
questions.explanation: 'Sanitation' (systems for waste disposal and hygiene) is the correct noun. 'Sanitising' is a verb form, 'sanitative' would be an adjective but is uncommon, and 'sanitarying' is incorrect.

questions.q: Which of these is the correct plural form of 'appendix' in a bibliography?
questions.explanation: The standard plural of 'appendix' (in formal writing) is 'appendices'. 'Appendixes' is sometimes used in general English but is less formal. 'Appendis' and 'appendiceses' are incorrect.

questions.q: Which word has the same initial consonant sound as the underlined consonant in "call" (the 'c' pronounced like 'k')?
questions.explanation: The initial 'c' in 'call' is pronounced /k/, which matches the initial sound of 'cat'. 'Cello' begins with /tʃ/ or /tʃɛ/ depending on accent, 'phone' begins with /f/, and 'church' begins with /tʃ/.

questions.q: Which pair of words share the same final consonant sound as in 'bag' (g as /g/)?
questions.explanation: 'Dog' and 'pig' both end with the voiced velar stop /g/, like 'bag'. 'Tap' and 'map' end with /p/ (voiceless bilabial), 'back' and 'pack' end with /k/ (voiceless velar), and 'bad' ends with /d/ while 'mat' ends with /t/.

questions.passage: Mr. Musa runs a small bakery by the busy Kano market. He opens before dawn to bake fresh buns and akara for traders who must leave early. Last Ramadan he extended his hours and sold large quantities of dates and bread to fasting customers after sunset. Business improved steadily after he introduced an online ordering number and began delivering within 5 km. Despite occasional power cuts, he keeps costs down by switching between mains electricity and a gas oven. Neighbours praise him for hiring local youths and for teaching apprentices the craft. He dreams of opening a second branch in Zaria within two years.
questions.q: According to the passage, which action most directly increased Mr. Musa's sales?
options: introducing an online ordering number and delivery within 5 km
switching between mains electricity and gas
questions.explanation: The passage states 'Business improved steadily after he introduced an online ordering number and began delivering within 5 km,' directly linking that action to increased sales. Extending Ramadan hours helped sales seasonally, while switching power sources and hiring youths are operational or social improvements, not identified as the main cause of increased business.

questions.passage: Mr. Musa runs a small bakery by the busy Kano market. He opens before dawn to bake fresh buns and akara for traders who must leave early. Last Ramadan he extended his hours and sold large quantities of dates and bread to fasting customers after sunset. questions.q: What does the phrase 'keeps costs down by switching between mains electricity and a gas oven' imply about Mr. Musa's approach to running the bakery?
options: He refuses to use electricity at all.
He uses flexible strategies to reduce operating expenses.
He relies only on generators regardless of price.
He wastes fuel by using both simultaneously.
questions.explanation: Switching between electricity and a gas oven suggests flexibility to minimise costs. It does not mean he refuses electricity, wastes fuel, or always uses generators; those options contradict the idea of switching to reduce expense.

questions.passage: Mr. Musa runs a small bakery by the busy Kano market. He opens before dawn to bake fresh buns and akara for traders who must leave early. Last Ramadan he extended his hours and sold large quantities of dates and bread to fasting customers after sunset. Despite occasional power cuts, he keeps costs down by switching between mains electricity and a gas oven. Neighbours praise him for hiring local youths and for teaching apprentices the craft. He dreams of opening a second branch in Zaria within two years.
questions.q: If a neighbour says of Mr. Musa, "He keeps his head above water," what do they mean?
options: He literally stays above floodwaters in raining seasons.
He manages to survive financially despite difficulties.
He spends most of his time swimming.
questions.explanation: The idiom 'keeps his head above water' means to cope financially or avoid failure. It does not refer to literal swimming or imply he refuses help; those are literal or unrelated interpretations.

questions.q: Choose the best meaning of the idiom: "to bite off more than you can chew" in this sentence — "When Raji started three side jobs while studying, his friends warned him not to bite off more than he could chew."
options: to take on more responsibilities than one can handle
questions.explanation: The idiom means taking on excessive tasks beyond one's capacity. The wrong options are literal readings unrelated to the idiom's figurative meaning.

questions.q: Choose the correct word to complete this sentence: "By the time the bank manager arrived, the customer ______ for over an hour."
questions.explanation: The past perfect continuous "had been waiting" is used to show an action (waiting) that began before a past reference point (the manager's arrival) and continued up to it. "Was waiting" could be acceptable in some contexts but does not emphasise the duration before the manager arrived. "Has waited" is present perfect and mismatches the past reference, while "will have waited" is future perfect and incorrect here.

questions.q: Choose the correct option to complete the sentence: "If Amina ______ earlier, she would have caught the 8:00 bus."
questions.explanation: This third conditional requires the past perfect "had left" to talk about an unreal past condition and its result. "Left" is simple past and doesn't form the third conditional. "Would leave" is incorrect because 'would' goes in the result clause, not the if-clause. "Has left" is present perfect and not suitable for a past counterfactual.

questions.passage: Mr. Adeyemi runs a small electronics shop in Ibadan near the university. For years he sold batteries and phone chargers, relying mostly on students who passed through on weekdays. When the new campus hostel opened, many students moved closer and fewer passed the old route, so he expected sales to fall. To adapt, he began selling low-cost power banks and offering quick phone-screen repairs. During the Egungun festival, visitors and parents came in larger numbers than usual. His income rose by twenty percent that month. He invested part of the extra naira into publicity leaflets and a simple generator to keep lights on during frequent power cuts. Neighbours praised his persistence, and some customers recommended him to others online.
questions.q: According to the passage, why did Mr. Adeyemi start selling power banks?
options: Because the university management forced him
Because his old stock of batteries was stolen
To adapt to fewer passers-by and meet changing demand
Because power banks were cheaper to buy in bulk
questions.explanation: The passage states he expected sales to fall after students moved and so adapted by selling power banks and offering repairs to meet new demand. There is no mention of bulk price benefits, university pressure, or theft of batteries, so those options are unsupported by the text.

Neighbours praised his persistence, and some customers recommended him to others online.
questions.q: Which phrase from the passage shows that Mr. Adeyemi took action to attract customers?
options: invested part of the extra naira into publicity leaflets
questions.explanation: The phrase about investing in publicity leaflets directly shows an action taken to attract customers. The other choices are background facts: running a shop is not a specific marketing action, students moving closer is context, and neighbours praising him is a reaction from others.

questions.q: What does the passage imply was the most direct reason for the 20% rise in income?
options: An immediate price increase on all goods
A long-term contract with the university
A government grant to small shops
Increased footfall during the Egungun festival
questions.explanation: The passage links larger numbers of visitors during the Egungun festival with his income rising by twenty percent that month, making this the most direct reason. There is no mention of price increases, government grants, or contracts with the university.

questions.q: Which of these words is stressed on the second syllable?
questions.explanation: "Arrival" is stressed on the second syllable (a-RRI-val). "Market" is stressed on the first syllable, "student" on the first, and "battery" on the first, so they are incorrect.

questions.q: Which sentence uses emphatic stress to contradict the suggestion that Mr. Adeyemi was careless with his business?
options: He did not spend all the extra money; he saved part of it for a generator.
People said he had bad luck with customers.
He spent the extra money on food for his family.
He had been careless for a long time.
questions.explanation: The correct sentence uses emphatic stress ('did not') to deny the suggestion and then gives evidence he saved money for a generator. The wrong options either agree with carelessness or don't contradict it with emphasis.

questions.q: Choose the best antonym of 'frequent' as used to describe the power cuts.
questions.explanation: 'Frequent' means happening often; the best antonym among the options is 'rare', meaning not happening often. 'Continuous', 'regular', and 'constant' all suggest ongoing or repeated occurrence and are near-synonyms, so they are incorrect.

questions.q: Choose the best synonym of 'praise' as used in the sentence 'Neighbours praised his persistence.'
questions.explanation: 'Praised' means expressed approval; 'commended' is an appropriate synonym. 'Blamed', 'ignored', and 'doubted' are antonyms or unrelated actions and therefore incorrect.

questions.q: Select the correct word to complete the sentence: "After the generator broke, business slowed ______ the shop could not keep lights on during the evening."
questions.explanation: "Because" introduces the reason for the slowdown (the shop could not keep lights on). "Although" would introduce a contrast and doesn't fit the stated cause. "Unless" and "if" introduce conditions, which are not appropriate here.

questions.q: Which word has the same initial consonant sound as the underlined consonant in 'cat' (c as /k/)?
questions.explanation: The letter c in 'cat' is pronounced /k/, the same initial sound as in 'king'. 'City' and 'chair' begin with /s/ and /tʃ/ respectively, and 'judge' begins with /dʒ/.

questions.passage: Mr. Okoro runs a small mobile-phone charging kiosk at the bus park in Enugu. Frequent power cuts and the rising price of diesel forced him to adapt: he bought a few solar panels and began offering short-term battery charging while passengers waited. Business picked up after he posted clear prices and charging times on a bright signboard. He also allowed customers to leave phones for longer charging at a lower rate. Within three months his takings rose noticeably, and he hired a young assistant to help during peak hours. Though the location is noisy, many commuters preferred his kiosk because it was reliable and cheaper than nearby shops.
questions.q: According to the passage, why did Mr. Okoro buy solar panels?
options: Because frequent power cuts and higher diesel prices made running a generator costly
To sell panels to commuters at a profit
Because the government required kiosks to use solar energy
To provide lighting for the bus park at night
questions.explanation: The passage states that frequent power cuts and rising diesel prices forced him to adapt, so buying solar panels reduced reliance on costly generators. The other choices are not mentioned or implied by the passage.

questions.q: Choose the correct form of the word to complete the sentence: "The assistant showed great ______ in managing the queue during rush hour."
questions.explanation: 'Patience' (a noun) correctly completes the sentence. 'Patient' is an adjective, 'patiencely' is not a standard adverb, and 'patienceful' is not a correct English word.

questions.q: Which word has the same vowel sound as the 'o' in "loan" (as in "loan")?
questions.explanation: The 'o' in 'loan' is the long /oʊ/ sound, which is the same as in 'go'. 'Hot' has /ɒ/ or /ɑ/ depending on accent, 'look' has /ʊ/, and 'love' has /ʌ/, so they are incorrect.

questions.q: Which pair of words share the same final consonant sound as in 'bus' (s as /s/)?
questions.explanation: 'Bus' ends with /s/; 'face' ends with the /s/ sound (written ce) and 'hiss' ends with /s/. 'Robe' ends with /b/ sound, 'give' with /v/, 'badge' and 'judge' end with /dʒ/, and 'bag'/'rag' with /g/.

questions.q: Which is the correct spelling to complete the sentence: "He offered a full _______ for the damaged phone."
questions.explanation: 'Refund' is the correct noun. 'Refunde' and 'refond' are misspellings, and 'refound' is the past participle of 'refind' or incorrect here.

questions.q: Which word contains the same middle consonant sound as the underlined consonant in 'banana' (the middle 'n' as /n/)?
questions.explanation: The middle 'n' in 'banana' is /n/; 'money' contains the /n/ sound in the middle. 'Badge' ends with /dʒ/, 'measure' has /ʒ/, and 'judge' begins with /dʒ/, so they do not match.

questions.q: Which word has the same vowel sound as the 'ea' in "heat" (as in "heat")?
questions.explanation: The 'ea' in 'heat' is the long /iː/ vowel, the same as in 'see'. 'Head', 'great', and 'bread' use the /ɛ/ vowel sound, so they are incorrect.

questions.q: Read the sentence: "After months of negotiation, the landlord finally relented and accepted the reduced rent." What does the word 'relented' most nearly mean in this sentence?
questions.explanation: Here 'relented' means the landlord yielded or 'gave in' to the request for reduced rent. 'Became firmer' is the opposite; 'repeated verbally' and 'set a deadline' do not fit the context of changing a stance.

questions.q: Which option best explains the meaning of the idiom: "to keep something under wraps"?
questions.explanation: "To keep something under wraps" idiomatically means to keep it secret or hidden. 'Store it carefully' and 'wrap it for presentation' are literal interpretations, while 'to damage it slightly' is unrelated.

questions.q: Choose the best word to complete the sentence: "If the market remains weak, traders ______ their stock until prices improve."
questions.explanation: The sentence is a first conditional about a likely future result: 'If the market remains weak, traders will hold their stock...' 'Holded' is nonstandard, 'would held' mixes modal forms incorrectly, and 'had held' is past perfect and incorrect for this future context.

questions.passage: Mrs. Olawale runs a small tailoring business in Ibadan. Last year she bought a sewing machine on hire purchase and rented a stall near the university gate. At first, students were slow to notice her, so she offered a 10% discount on uniforms during the first month. Word spread, and soon orders increased. To meet demand she took on an apprentice and extended her opening hours until late in the evening. Her expenses rose, but so did income: after six months she cleared a small profit and paid off the hire-purchase balance. Encouraged, Mrs. Olawale plans to train two more apprentices and save for a second machine.
questions.q: According to the passage, which action most directly helped Mrs. Olawale increase her orders?
options: renting a stall near the university gate
buying a sewing machine on hire purchase
offering a 10% discount during the first month
questions.explanation: The passage states that students were slow to notice her, so she offered a 10% discount and 'Word spread, and soon orders increased.' Thus the discount most directly triggered the rise in orders. Buying the machine and renting the stall were important but not described as the immediate cause; taking an apprentice responded to increased demand rather than causing it.
